title: Undoing a pushed commit with git revert
text: git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier commit. Because it adds history instead of rewriting it, revert is the safe way to undo a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch. Teammates just pull the new revert commit; nothing they have breaks.

title: git reset and throwing away local work
text: git reset moves the current branch pointer to another commit. With --soft the working tree and index are kept, with --mixed the index is cleared, and with --hard all uncommitted local changes are discarded permanently. Because reset rewrites branch history it is dangerous on branches other people share.

title: Rebasing to keep history linear
text: git rebase replays your commits on top of another base commit, producing a linear history without merge commits. Never rebase commits that others have already pulled: rebasing rewrites commit hashes and forces everyone downstream to recover manually.

title: Resolving merge conflicts
text: When two branches change the same lines, git stops and writes conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into the affected files. Edit each file to keep the content you want, remove the markers, then git add the file and continue the merge or rebase. A merge tool can show both sides next to each other.

title: Shelving work in progress with git stash
text: git stash takes your uncommitted changes, saves them on a stack, and restores a clean working tree. It is the quickest way to temporarily set aside half-done work without making a commit, switch branches, and later bring the changes back with git stash pop.

title: Copying a single commit with cherry-pick
text: git cherry-pick takes one existing commit from another branch and applies the same change as a new commit on your current branch. It is useful for pulling a specific bug fix into a release branch without merging everything else.

title: Finding the bad commit with git bisect
text: git bisect runs a binary search over your commit history to find which commit introduced a bug. You mark one commit as good and one as bad, then git checks out the midpoint and you test and mark it, halving the range each step until the first bad commit is identified.

title: Searching history for a change with git log -S
text: git log -S, the pickaxe, finds commits that added or removed a given string. It answers questions like: when did this function disappear, or which commit introduced this constant. Combine with -p to see the patches.

title: How Docker image layers work
text: Every instruction in a Dockerfile produces an image layer. Layers stack on each other and are content-addressed, so identical layers are stored and downloaded once. Rebuilds reuse unchanged layers from the build cache, which is why instruction order matters so much for build speed.

title: Ordering Dockerfile instructions for cache hits
text: The Docker build cache reuses a layer only if the instruction and all layers before it are unchanged. Copy dependency manifests and install packages before copying the rest of the source, so editing application code does not invalidate the expensive install layer. Getting this order right is the main lever for faster builds.

title: Multi-stage builds for small images
text: A multi-stage build uses one stage with compilers and build tools to produce artifacts, then copies only those artifacts into a minimal final stage. The final image ships without the toolchain, which shrinks image size dramatically and reduces the attack surface.

title: Persisting container data with volumes
text: Container filesystems are ephemeral: when the container is removed its writable layer is gone. A named volume or bind mount stores data outside the container lifecycle, so a database keeps its files across container restarts and recreation. Named volumes are managed by Docker; bind mounts map a host directory.

title: Container-to-container networking
text: Containers on the same user-defined bridge network can reach each other using the container or service name as the hostname; Docker runs an embedded DNS server that resolves those names. The default bridge does not offer name resolution, which is a common source of connection refused surprises.

title: Running multi-container apps with Compose
text: Docker Compose describes an application as services in a YAML file: images, ports, volumes, environment, and dependencies between services. One command starts the whole stack, and services automatically share a network where they address each other by service name.

title: Virtual environments for Python projects
text: A virtual environment gives each Python project its own interpreter and site-packages directory, isolating its dependencies from the system and from other projects. Create one with python -m venv, activate it, and pip installs stay contained. Deleting the directory removes everything cleanly.

title: Pinning dependencies for reproducible installs
text: Pinning exact package versions in a requirements or lock file makes installs reproducible: the same versions resolve on every machine and in CI. Unpinned ranges drift, and a transitive upgrade can break a build that worked yesterday. Regenerate the lock file deliberately, not implicitly.

title: The GIL and CPU-bound Python threads
text: CPython's global interpreter lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help for I/O waiting, but CPU-bound work on threads will not use multiple cores. For parallel computation use multiprocessing or a native extension that releases the GIL.

title: asyncio for I/O-bound concurrency
text: asyncio runs many tasks on a single thread with an event loop: while one task awaits a network response, others make progress. It suits workloads dominated by waiting, like calling many HTTP APIs concurrently. It does nothing for CPU-bound work, and one blocking call stalls the whole loop.

title: Generators for lazy iteration
text: A generator function yields items one at a time instead of building a whole list in memory. Iterating a huge file line by line through a generator pipeline keeps memory flat no matter the file size. Generators are single-pass: once consumed, you must recreate them.

title: Choosing HTTP status codes
text: 2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx a client error, 5xx a server error. Use 400 for a malformed request, 401 when authentication is missing, 403 when it is present but insufficient, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for a conflict, and 500 only for genuine server faults.

title: HTTP caching with Cache-Control and ETags
text: The Cache-Control header tells browsers and proxies how long a response stays fresh: max-age sets the lifetime, no-store forbids storing. After expiry the client revalidates with an ETag or Last-Modified validator, and the server answers 304 Not Modified if the content is unchanged, saving the transfer.

title: Idempotent HTTP methods and safe retries
text: An idempotent request can be sent twice with the same effect as once: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not. That is what makes retrying a timed-out PUT safe, while retrying a POST risks creating a duplicate. For POST, an idempotency key lets the server deduplicate.

title: Rate limiting and 429 responses
text: When a client exceeds its request quota the server responds 429 Too Many Requests, often with a Retry-After header saying how long to wait. Well-behaved clients back off exponentially and add jitter so a crowd of clients does not retry in synchronized waves.

title: CORS and the same-origin policy
text: Browsers block scripts from reading responses fetched from a different origin unless the server opts in. The server grants access with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and for non-simple requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight. CORS errors are a browser protection; curl and server-to-server calls never see them.

title: Stateless authentication with JWTs
text: A JSON Web Token carries signed claims about the user, so the server can verify a request without a session store: authentication state lives in the token itself. Keep lifetimes short and pair the access token with a refresh token, because a signed token cannot be revoked before it expires without extra infrastructure.

title: Database indexes and query speed
text: A B-tree index lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table, turning a slow query into a fast lookup. Indexes cost write time and storage, so index the columns your queries actually filter and join on. In a composite index column order decides which queries it can serve.

title: The N+1 query problem
text: An ORM that loads a list and then lazily fetches a relation per row issues one query for the list plus N more, one per item. The fix is eager loading: fetch the relation with a join or a single batched query. The symptom is a page that gets slower linearly as the list grows.

title: Transactions and isolation
text: A transaction groups statements so they commit or roll back as one atomic unit, keeping the database consistent when something fails halfway. Isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency: read committed allows non-repeatable reads, serializable prevents anomalies but retries more.

title: Connection pooling
text: Opening a database connection is expensive, so applications keep a pool of open connections and lease them per request. Under heavy concurrent load an undersized pool exhausts and requests queue waiting for a free connection, while an oversized pool overwhelms the database. Pool exhaustion often looks like random timeouts.

title: Versioned schema migrations
text: Schema migrations are ordered, versioned scripts that evolve the database structure alongside the code. Each migration has a forward step and ideally a rollback, and a version table records what has run, so every environment converges on the same schema.

title: Searching file contents with grep
text: grep searches text for lines matching a pattern. Use -r to search every file under a directory recursively, -i to ignore case, -n for line numbers, and -l to list only matching file names. It is the fastest way to find where a string appears in a codebase.

title: Locating files with find
text: find walks a directory tree and matches files by name, type, size, or modification time: find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7 lists log files older than a week. Add -exec to run a command on each match. find locates files by their attributes; grep searches inside their contents.

title: Pipes and command composition
text: A pipe connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin, so small tools compose into pipelines: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn. Each command runs concurrently, and by default the pipeline's exit status is the last command's; set -o pipefail makes earlier failures visible.

title: SSH key authentication
text: SSH key authentication replaces passwords with a key pair: the public key goes into authorized_keys on the server, and the private key stays on your machine to sign a challenge at login. An ssh-agent holds the decrypted key so you do not retype the passphrase for every connection.

title: Scheduling jobs with cron
text: A crontab entry has five time fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, then the command. 0 3 * * * runs every night at 03:00. Cron jobs run with a minimal environment and no interactive PATH, which is why a job that works in your shell can silently fail under cron.

title: Configuration in environment variables
text: Keep configuration and secrets in environment variables, not in source code or the repository. The same build then runs in every environment with different settings, credentials never land in version control history, and rotating a secret does not require a deploy of new code.

title: Redis as an application cache
text: Redis stores hot data in memory so reads skip the database. Give every entry a TTL so stale values expire on their own, and pick an eviction policy such as allkeys-lru for when memory fills up. The classic pattern is cache-aside: read the cache first, on a miss load from the database and write back.

title: Load balancers
text: A load balancer spreads incoming requests across multiple server instances and health-checks each one, routing around instances that stop responding. Round robin and least-connections are the common strategies. It is the component that lets a service scale horizontally behind one address.

title: Caching at every layer
text: Caching shows up at every layer of a system. The browser cache keeps assets on the user's disk. A CDN cache serves content from edge locations near users. An application cache like Redis holds hot objects in memory. The database cache keeps pages in its buffer pool. Each cache layer trades freshness for speed, and every cache needs an invalidation story: TTL expiry, explicit purge, or versioned keys. The hardest bugs in a cache-heavy system come from stale cache entries and from cache stampedes, where many requests miss the cache at once and pile onto the backend. A useful habit is to ask, for every cache you add: what fills the cache, what invalidates the cache, and what happens when the cache is cold. Caching is a performance multiplier, but a cache is also a second copy of the truth, and second copies drift.

title: Production operations glossary
text: A working vocabulary for running services in production. Logs are timestamped event records; centralize them and make them searchable. Metrics are numeric time series like request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles; alerts fire when metrics cross thresholds. Tracing follows one request across services. Deploys ship new versions; a rollback returns to the previous version; a canary sends a small slice of traffic to the new version first. Containers package applications with their dependencies; an orchestrator schedules containers across machines and restarts failed containers. A database stores durable state and needs backups you have actually tested restoring. A queue buffers work between services and smooths traffic spikes. An incident is any unplanned degradation; a postmortem records what happened, why the system allowed it, and which changes prevent a repeat. On-call rotations spread that responsibility, and runbooks turn tribal knowledge into checklists anyone can follow under pressure.
